I put the receipt email behind a flag in `services/notifier/notifier/email.py`. When `NOTIFIER_FF_NEW_RECEIPT_EMAIL=1`, `send_receipt` renders the template `receipt_v2`. When it's unset or any other value, it uses the current `receipt` template, so nothing changes until someone turns it on.

The notifier is deployed separately and can't read the root `flags.toml` or `flags.is_on()`. So the flag is an environment variable, following the notifier's `NOTIFIER_FF_<NAME>` convention.

I added a test for the flag-on path and made the existing test clear the variable first; both tests pass. Nothing is committed yet.

Three things to check:

- **The new email isn't in the repo.** I couldn't find a new receipt template or any work on one, on any branch or stash, and there's no `templates/` directory at all. I made up the name `receipt_v2` for it. If the new email is somewhere else or has a different name, tell me and I'll change it. Whoever adds it will need both `templates/receipt_v2.mjml` and a plain-text `receipt_v2.txt` using the same variables (`invoice_id`, `total_minor`).
- **The rollout is all-or-nothing per deployment.** Because it's a single environment variable, it can't send the new email to just a share of customers; you can only switch it on one deployment at a time (staging first, then production). If you want a percentage rollout, I can add a stable bucket based on the invoice ID.
- **Only the email body changes.** The subject line is still "Your receipt" either way. If the new email has its own subject, that needs to go behind the flag too.

One thing was awkward; nothing actually blocked me.

**The hook's injected context left out each memory's physical scope.** The prompt hook gave me two feature-flag conventions that conflict:

- "Feature flags go through flags.is_on()", declared in `flags.toml`
- "Feature flags in the notifier", using `NOTIFIER_FF_<NAME>` environment variables

Each one was shown with only its type, id, source and text. I picked the notifier convention because its text says the notifier can't read the root `flags.toml`. But nothing in the injected block showed that the `flags.is_on()` memory covers only the billing app (for example `src/`) and the notifier memory covers `services/notifier/`.

I would have wanted the hook output to include each memory's `physical` and `logical` scopes, which `create` already stores. I'd have used them to confirm the right flag convention for the file I was editing, without depending on how a memory happened to be worded. I could have called `query` with `path` set to `services/notifier/notifier/email.py`, or `get` on both ids, to check. So this was a missing convenience in the injected context, not a missing capability.

I also never ran a `query` or saved anything at the end. For example, I could have recorded that the notifier has no `templates/` directory yet, despite the template convention. That was my choice, not a gap in the tools.
